obj: Name the bones of the neurocranium and viscerocranium
Locate the pterion and explain its clinical importance
Identify the bones that form the cranial base
Describe the mandible and its joint with the temporal bone
Locate the paranasal sinuses

steps.x: The neurocranium protects the brain. Its vault is formed by the frontal bone, both parietal bones and the squamous part of the occipital, joined by the coronal, sagittal and lambdoid sutures.
At the pterion the frontal, parietal, temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid meet. The bone is thin here: a fracture can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an epidural haematoma.

The base is formed by the ethmoid, sphenoid, temporal and occipital bones. The foramen magnum of the occipital transmits the medulla oblongata. The petrous part of the temporal houses the middle and inner ear.

The viscerocranium is the skeleton of the face. The maxillae carry the upper teeth and, with the palatine bones, form the hard palate. Zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, inferior nasal concha and vomer complete the facial skeleton.
The mandible is the only movable bone of the skull. Its condyle articulates with the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint. Its body holds the lower teeth.

The frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxilla contain air spaces that drain into the nasal cavity. Maxillary sinusitis can mimic toothache, because the roots of the upper molars lie next to the sinus floor.

Which bones meet at the pterion?

t: Vertebral column: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacrum and coccyx
obj: List the regions of the spine and their number of vertebrae
Distinguish cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae by their features
Describe the atlas and axis and the movements they allow
Describe the sacrum and coccyx
Relate the intervertebral disc to disc herniation

steps.x: The spine has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx. In side view it shows cervical and lumbar lordosis and thoracic and sacral kyphosis, which absorb load.
The atlas (C1) has no body: it is a ring whose lateral masses receive the occipital condyles (the "yes" movement). The axis (C2) bears the dens, around which the atlas rotates (the "no" movement).

From C3 to C7 the body is small and the transverse processes contain a foramen transversarium. The vertebral artery ascends through it, usually entering at C6. C7, the vertebra prominens, has the most palpable spinous process.
They have heart-shaped bodies and costal facets on the body and transverse processes for the ribs. Their spinous processes are long and slope downward.

Lumbar vertebrae have large, kidney-shaped bodies, with no foramina transversaria or costal facets. Disc herniations are most common at L4–L5 and L5–S1: the nucleus pulposus bulges posterolaterally and compresses the descending root (L5 in an L4–L5 herniation).

The sacrum results from the fusion of 5 vertebrae. Its base forms the promontory and its auricular surfaces articulate with the hip bones. The coccyx, 3 to 5 rudimentary vertebrae, joins the sacrum at the sacrococcygeal symphysis.

Which feature is unique to cervical vertebrae?

obj: Describe the components of the thoracic cage
Identify the parts of the sternum and the sternal angle
Distinguish true, false and floating ribs
Describe a typical rib and its posterior joints
Apply the anatomy of the costal groove to thoracentesis

steps.x: It is formed by 12 thoracic vertebrae, 12 pairs of ribs with their costal cartilages, and the sternum. It protects the heart and lungs and moves with breathing.

It has a manubrium, body and xiphoid process. The manubrium articulates with the clavicles and the first costal cartilages. Its junction with the body forms the palpable sternal angle, at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage: it is used to count ribs.
The first seven ribs join the sternum directly through their own costal cartilage. That is why they are called true or vertebrosternal ribs.
Ribs 8, 9 and 10 join their cartilage to the one above and form the costal margin. Ribs 11 and 12 are floating: their anterior end lies free in the abdominal wall.

The head articulates with two vertebral bodies and the tubercle with the transverse process of its own vertebra. Along the lower border, the costal groove holds the intercostal vein, artery and nerve. In thoracentesis the needle passes over the upper border of the lower rib.
show: Radiate ligament of head of rib
Intra-articular ligament of head of rib

steps.x: It is the shortest, broadest and most curved rib. Its upper surface has the scalene tubercle, which separates the grooves for the subclavian vein and artery.

q.p: At what level is the sternal angle?
Which ribs are floating ribs?
What does the costal groove contain?
In thoracentesis, where is the needle inserted?
o: Over the upper border of the lower rib
Under the lower border of the upper rib
In the middle of the space, with no landmark

q.p: What does the tubercle of a typical rib articulate with?
o: The body of the vertebra above
The transverse process of its own vertebra

obj: Identify the bones of the shoulder girdle and their joints
Describe the main features of the scapula
Describe the proximal humerus, shaft and distal end
Relate humeral fractures to the nerves at risk

steps.x: The clavicle and scapula attach the upper limb to the trunk. The only bony joint with the axial skeleton is the sternoclavicular joint, between the clavicle and the manubrium.
It is an S-shaped bone that acts as a strut between the sternum and the acromion. It is the first bone to ossify and one of the most frequently fractured, mainly in its middle third.

It is a flat, triangular bone. On its posterior surface, the spine separates the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and ends laterally as the acromion. The anterior surface forms the subscapular fossa.
The glenoid cavity is shallow; the glenoid labrum deepens it. The coracoid process gives attachment to pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps.

Head, anatomical neck and greater and lesser tubercles, separated by the intertubercular groove, which carries the tendon of the long head of biceps. A fracture of the surgical neck can injure the axillary nerve.

On the posterior shaft lies the radial groove: a fracture here can cause wrist drop. Distally, the capitulum and trochlea articulate with radius and ulna; the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle.

q.p: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus puts which nerve at risk?
A humeral shaft fracture with wrist drop indicates injury to which nerve?
Which joint is the only bony link between the upper limb and the axial skeleton?
What runs in the intertubercular groove of the humerus?
o: The tendon of the long head of biceps

q.p: Which structure separates the supraspinous from the infraspinous fossa?

t: Bones of the forearm and hand
obj: Identify the radius and ulna and their ends
Name the eight carpal bones in their two rows
Describe the metacarpals and phalanges
Explain the typical fractures of the distal radius and scaphoid

steps.x: In the anatomical position the ulna is medial and the radius lateral. The interosseous membrane joins them. In pronation, the radius rotates and crosses in front of the ulna.
Its proximal end has the olecranon and coronoid process, which form the trochlear notch that grips the humeral trochlea. The olecranon is the point of the elbow.

Its head rotates within the annular ligament against the ulna. The distal end is broad and articulates with the carpus. A Colles fracture, from a fall on the outstretched hand, affects the distal radius with dorsal displacement.
From lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform. The scaphoid is the most often fractured; its blood supply enters distally, so the proximal fragment may undergo necrosis.
From lateral to medial: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate. With the proximal row they form the carpal tunnel, roofed by the flexor retinaculum.
Five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges: the thumb has two and the other fingers three (proximal, middle and distal). The highly mobile first metacarpal allows thumb opposition.
show: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
Distal phalanx of first finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Distal phalanx of third finger of hand

q.p: Which carpal bone is fractured most often?
After a scaphoid fracture, which fragment is at greater risk of avascular necrosis?
o: The proximal one, because its blood supply comes from distal
The distal one, because it has no attachments
The proximal one, because the ulnar artery supplies it

q.p: Which part of the ulna forms the point of the elbow?
How many phalanges does the thumb have?
q.en: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

q.p: A Colles fracture affects…
o: The distal radius with palmar displacement
The distal radius with dorsal displacement

t: Bony pelvis: hip bone, sacrum and sex differences
obj: Identify the bones and joints of the pelvic ring
Describe the parts of the hip bone and the acetabulum
Explain how the greater and lesser sciatic foramina are formed
Distinguish the male from the female pelvis
Relate the diameters of the lesser pelvis to childbirth

steps.x: It is formed by the two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx. Anteriorly, the pubic bones meet at the pubic symphysis; posteriorly, each hip bone articulates with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint.

It results from the fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis, which unite at the acetabulum during adolescence. Key landmarks are the iliac crest, the anterior superior iliac spine and the ischial tuberosity, which bears weight when sitting.

The acetabulum receives the femoral head; the acetabular labrum deepens it and the transverse ligament bridges its notch. Below, the obturator membrane closes the obturator foramen except for the canal for the obturator vessels and nerve.

The auricular surfaces of the sacrum and ilium meet with very little movement. The joint is reinforced by the anterior, posterior and interosseous sacroiliac ligaments; the interosseous is the strongest.

The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. The sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below piriformis.

steps.t: Greater and lesser pelvis, and sex
steps.x: The linea terminalis separates the greater from the lesser pelvis. In women the pelvic inlet is more oval, the lesser pelvis wider and shallower, and the subpubic angle wider. The obstetric conjugate is the key diameter in childbirth.

q.p: Which bones fuse at the acetabulum?
Which feature is typical of the female pelvis?
Through which opening does the sciatic nerve leave the pelvis?
Which sacroiliac ligament is the strongest?
Which diameter of the lesser pelvis matters most in childbirth?
o: Distance between the anterior superior iliac spines

obj: Describe the ends and shaft of the femur
Explain the role of the patella as a sesamoid bone
Distinguish the tibia and fibula by shape and function
Relate femoral neck and fibular neck fractures to their complications

steps.x: Head, neck and greater and lesser trochanters; the neck makes an angle of about 125° with the shaft. The head is supplied mainly by branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery: a neck fracture in older adults can cause avascular necrosis.

The femur is the longest bone in the body. Posteriorly, the linea aspera receives the adductors, vasti and the short head of biceps femoris. Distally, the medial and lateral condyles are separated by the intercondylar fossa.

It is the largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon. It glides on the patellar surface of the femur and increases the lever arm of quadriceps. The patellar ligament joins it to the tibia.

It is the weight-bearing bone of the leg and lies medially. Its plateau carries the menisci; the tibial tuberosity receives the patellar ligament and the medial malleolus forms part of the ankle. Its medial surface is subcutaneous, so it is the long bone most often involved in open fractures.

It is slender, lateral and bears little weight; it serves mainly for muscle attachment. Its distal end forms the lateral malleolus, lower than the medial one. The common fibular nerve winds around its neck: injury causes foot drop.

q.p: Which artery provides most of the blood supply to the adult femoral head?
o: Artery of the ligament of the head

q.p: What type of bone is the patella?
A fibular neck fracture with foot drop indicates injury to which nerve?
Where does the patellar ligament attach?
Which posterior ridge of the femur receives the adductor muscles?

obj: Name the seven tarsal bones
Describe the talus and calcaneus and their role in weight-bearing
Identify the metatarsals, phalanges and sesamoids
Relate foot fractures to their mechanism and complications

steps.x: The foot has 26 main bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges. The hindfoot is formed by the talus and calcaneus; the rest of the tarsus by the navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms.
show: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot

steps.x: Its trochlea fits into the mortise formed by tibia and fibula and transmits the weight of the leg to the foot. It has no muscle attachments and is largely covered by cartilage: its blood supply is fragile and a neck fracture can cause necrosis.

It is the largest tarsal bone and forms the heel. Its tuberosity receives the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon and its sustentaculum supports the talus medially. It fractures in falls from height onto the heels.

The navicular lies in front of the talus on the medial side; its tuberosity receives tibialis posterior. The cuboid is lateral and has a groove for the fibularis longus tendon. The three cuneiforms articulate with the first three metatarsals.

They are five long bones with base, shaft and head. The tuberosity of the 5th receives fibularis brevis and can be avulsed in an inversion sprain. The 2nd metatarsal is a typical site of stress fractures.
The big toe has two phalanges and the others three. Beneath the head of the 1st metatarsal lie two sesamoids, in the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis, which protect and spread the load.
show: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Distal phalanx of first finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot
Middle phalanx of second finger of foot
Distal phalanx of second finger of foot

q.p: Which tarsal bone has no muscle attachments?
Where does the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon insert?
Which muscle inserts on the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal?
In which bone are stress fractures of the foot most typical?
How many bones form the tarsus?

steps.x: The femur articulates with the tibia and the patella. The fibula does not take part in the knee joint, but serves as an anchor for the fibular collateral ligament.
The anterior cruciate prevents the tibia from sliding forward; the posterior, backward. They are examined with the Lachman and drawer tests.
The tibial collateral resists valgus and is attached to the medial meniscus; the fibular collateral resists varus and is extracapsular.
show: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

steps.x: C-shaped fibrocartilages that distribute load. The medial one, less mobile because of its attachment to the tibial collateral, is injured more often.
The patellar ligament joins the patella to the tibial tuberosity, and the retinacula stabilize it at the sides.

q.p: Which structure prevents anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur?
Which meniscus is injured more often, and why?
o: The lateral, because it is larger
The lateral, because it is attached to the fibular collateral
The medial, because it is attached to the tibial collateral

q.p: Which ligament resists varus stress at the knee?
Which bone does not take part in the knee joint?

obj: Identify the bones that form the knee joint
Describe the function of the cruciate and collateral ligaments
Explain why the medial meniscus is injured more often
Relate each ligament to its clinical test

steps.x: The tibiofibular mortise embraces the talus. The lateral malleolus descends lower than the medial one and blocks eversion, while the shorter medial malleolus leaves inversion freer: that is why inversion sprains predominate.
It runs from the lateral malleolus to the neck of the talus and is tensed in plantar flexion and inversion. It is the first and most frequently injured.
The calcaneofibular ligament is injured in moderate sprains; the posterior talofibular, the strongest, only in severe ones.
The tibiofibular ligaments join the tibia and fibula. Their injury, the high ankle sprain, takes longer to heal.
The fibularis longus and brevis evert the foot and protect against inversion; their tendons pass under the fibular retinacula.

q.p: Which ligament is most often injured in a lateral ankle sprain?
In which position is the anterior talofibular ligament most taut?
Which muscles actively protect the ankle against inversion?
The so-called "high ankle sprain" affects…
o: The tibiofibular ligaments of the syndesmosis

q.p: Which lateral ligament, the strongest, tears only in severe sprains?

obj: Describe the ankle mortise and its relation to the talus
Identify the lateral ankle ligaments and their order of injury
Differentiate a lateral sprain from a syndesmotic sprain
Explain the role of the fibularis muscles as dynamic stabilisers

steps.x: Five large-bodied vertebrae bear the greatest axial load and form the lumbar lordosis over the sacrum.
The nucleus pulposus, surrounded by the annulus fibrosus, distributes the load. L4–L5 and L5–S1 account for most herniations.

The anterior longitudinal ligament limits extension; the posterior, weaker at the lumbar level, explains why herniations are posterolateral. The ligamenta flava, interspinous and supraspinous ligaments limit flexion.
It arises from L4 to S3 and descends through the gluteal region and the posterior thigh. Compression of its roots by a herniation produces sciatica.

q.p: At which levels do most lumbar disc herniations occur?
Why are lumbar herniations usually posterolateral?
o: Because the ligamentum flavum is weaker laterally
Because the anulus fibrosus is absent posteriorly
Because the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and weak at that level
Because the anterior longitudinal ligament pushes the disc backward

Which roots form the sciatic nerve?
In a disc herniation, which part of the disc protrudes and compresses the nerve root?

obj: Identify the lumbar vertebrae, sacrum and intervertebral discs
Describe the structure of the disc: nucleus pulposus and anulus fibrosus
Explain the function of the vertebral ligaments
Relate posterolateral disc herniation to sciatica
Identify the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints
Describe the capsule, labrum and glenohumeral ligaments
Differentiate the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments by function
Explain why glenohumeral dislocation is usually anteroinferior

steps.x: The large humeral head rests on a small, shallow glenoid cavity. The fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum widens and deepens it. It is the most mobile joint in the body and also the one that dislocates most often.

The capsule is lax and is reinforced anteriorly by the superior, middle and inferior glenohumeral ligaments. The inferior one is the main anterior restraint in abduction and external rotation. The coracohumeral ligament reinforces the upper part.

The coracoacromial ligament and the acromion form a roof that prevents superior dislocation of the humeral head. The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath it, protected by the subacromial bursa. Repeated friction causes subacromial pain syndrome.

The rotator cuff tendons blend with the capsule and centre the head in the glenoid. The inferior part of the capsule has no muscular reinforcement, so most dislocations are anteroinferior. The axillary nerve, just below, can be injured.

A plane synovial joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the acromion; it sometimes has an incomplete disc. The acromioclavicular ligament reinforces the capsule superiorly and controls horizontal displacement.

Its conoid and trapezoid parts join the coracoid process to the inferior surface of the clavicle. They are the main vertical stabiliser: they suspend the scapula from the clavicle. They also tear in severe acromioclavicular dislocations.

A saddle synovial joint divided by a disc into two cavities. It is the only articular link between the upper limb and the axial skeleton. The costoclavicular ligament is its main restraint; posterior dislocation can compress the great vessels.

q.p: What is the main vertical stabiliser of the acromioclavicular joint?
Which ligament is the main anterior restraint of the shoulder in abduction and external rotation?
After an anterior shoulder dislocation, which nerve is most often injured?
Which structure lies between the coracoacromial arch and the supraspinatus tendon?
How is the sternoclavicular joint classified?
o: Plane synovial joint without a disc
Saddle synovial joint with an articular disc

obj: Identify the humero-ulnar, humeroradial and radio-ulnar joints
Describe the collateral ligaments and the annular ligament
Explain the mechanism of pronation and supination
Relate the annular ligament to pulled elbow in children

steps.x: The humeral trochlea articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna (hinge) and the capitulum with the radial head. The proximal radio-ulnar joint completes the complex. All three share the same joint cavity.

The capsule is thin anteriorly and posteriorly, allowing wide flexion and extension. At the sides it is reinforced by the collateral ligaments. In extension, the olecranon fits into its fossa and locks the movement.

Triangular, it runs from the medial epicondyle to the coronoid process and olecranon. Its anterior band is the main restraint to valgus stress. It is injured in throwers; the ulnar nerve passes just behind the medial epicondyle.

The radial collateral ligament runs from the lateral epicondyle to the annular ligament. The annular ligament encircles the radial head and attaches to the margins of the radial notch of the ulna. In young children a pull on the arm can slip the radial head out of it: pulled elbow.

The ulnar head articulates with the ulnar notch of the radius. A triangular articular disc joins the radius to the base of the ulnar styloid process and separates the ulna from the carpus. The dorsal and palmar radio-ulnar ligaments reinforce it.
show: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

steps.x: In pronation the radius rotates and crosses in front of the ulna, which stays almost fixed. Supinator and biceps, strong with the elbow flexed, supinate; pronator teres and quadratus pronate. The interosseous membrane joins both bones and transfers load from radius to ulna.

q.p: Which structure separates the ulnar head from the carpal bones?
o: Articular disc of the distal radio-ulnar joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist
q.en: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

q.p: Which ligament mainly resists valgus stress at the elbow?
Which muscle is the most powerful supinator with the elbow flexed?
A 3-year-old stops using the arm after being pulled by the hand. What has probably happened?
o: Tear of the ulnar collateral ligament
Subluxation of the radial head out of the annular ligament

q.p: What type of joint is the proximal radio-ulnar joint?

t: Wrist and joints of the hand
obj: Describe the articular surfaces of the radiocarpal joint
Identify the extrinsic and intrinsic carpal ligaments
Explain the mobility of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb
Relate the metacarpophalangeal collateral ligaments to the position of immobilisation

steps.x: An ellipsoid joint between the radius and articular disc above and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum below. The ulna does not contact the carpus. It allows flexion, extension and radial and ulnar deviation.
show: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

steps.x: The palmar ligaments, thicker than the dorsal ones, run from the radius and ulna to the carpal bones. The radioscaphocapitate ligament supports the scaphoid. They make the carpus follow the radius in pronation and supination.

The dorsal radiocarpal and dorsal intercarpal ligaments reinforce the posterior surface. The radial collateral runs from the radial styloid to the scaphoid; the ulnar collateral, from the ulnar styloid to the triquetrum and pisiform. They limit side-to-side deviation.
show: Radial collateral ligament of wrist joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

steps.x: They bind the proximal row bones together, which move as a unit over the distal row at the midcarpal joint. Rupture of the scapholunate ligament separates both bones on X-ray and causes carpal instability.
The trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal form a saddle joint. It allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and opposition. It is a common site of osteoarthritis, especially in women.

Metacarpophalangeal joints are condylar; their collateral ligaments tighten in flexion, so the hand is immobilised with them flexed. Interphalangeal joints are hinges. Palmar plates limit hyperextension.
show: Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints

q.p: What type of joint is the radiocarpal joint?
An X-ray shows an abnormal gap between the scaphoid and lunate. Which ligament is torn?
The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, which allows opposition, is a…
Why are metacarpophalangeal joints immobilised in flexion?
o: Their collateral ligaments are taut in flexion and do not shorten
The capsule is thicker in extension
The palmar plate tears in flexion

q.p: Which forearm bone does not directly contact the carpus?
o: Both: the carpus only touches the disc

obj: Describe the articular surfaces of the hip joint
Identify the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments
Explain the blood supply of the femoral head
Relate femoral neck fracture to avascular necrosis

steps.x: The femoral head fits into the deep acetabulum: a very stable ball-and-socket joint. The fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum increases its depth. The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch.

It attaches to the acetabular rim and, anteriorly, to the intertrochanteric line. Posteriorly it does not reach the intertrochanteric crest, so part of the neck lies outside it. It is thick and strong, especially in front.

The Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament runs from the anterior inferior iliac spine to the intertrochanteric line. It is the strongest ligament in the body and limits extension, allowing standing with little muscle effort. The pubofemoral ligament limits abduction.

It reinforces the capsule posteriorly, running from the ischium upward and laterally. It is the weakest of the three. It limits internal rotation; in extension all three ligaments wind up and tighten.

steps.t: Blood supply of the femoral head
steps.x: The ligament of the head of the femur adds little stability and carries a branch of the obturator artery, important in children. In adults the head depends mainly on retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery; the lateral one contributes less. Their injury in neck fractures causes avascular necrosis.

The short lateral rotators cover the capsule posteriorly. Gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, keep the pelvis level in single-leg stance. If they fail, the pelvis drops on the opposite side: Trendelenburg sign.

q.p: Which ligament, the strongest in the body, limits hip extension?
o: Ligament of the head of the femur

q.p: In adults, which artery supplies most of the blood to the femoral head?
Which fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the acetabulum?
o: Ligament of the head of the femur

q.p: Which complication is typical of a displaced femoral neck fracture?
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

q.p: A positive Trendelenburg sign suggests injury to…

obj: Identify the articular surfaces and disc of the TMJ
Differentiate the movements of each joint compartment
Describe the ligaments of the TMJ
Relate the muscles of mastication to mandibular movements
Explain the mechanism of mandibular dislocation

steps.x: The head of the mandible articulates with the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone. Its surfaces are covered with fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage. Both TMJs always work together.

A biconcave disc divides the joint into two compartments. Forward gliding occurs in the upper one; rotation of the mandibular head occurs in the lower one. Part of the lateral pterygoid attaches to the disc and capsule.

The capsule is lax, especially above. The lateral ligament, a lateral thickening of the capsule, runs from the zygomatic arch to the neck of the mandible. It is the main reinforcement and prevents posterior displacement of the mandibular head.

The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible. The stylomandibular ligament runs from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible and limits excessive protrusion. Both add little strength to the joint.
Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid elevate the mandible and close the mouth. The lateral pterygoid pulls it forward and helps open it. All are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

On wide opening, the mandibular head and disc move forward onto the articular tubercle. If they pass beyond it (yawning, a blow), the mandible dislocates anteriorly and the mouth cannot close. It is reduced by pushing down and back.

q.p: In which TMJ compartment does forward gliding occur?
Which muscle protrudes the mandible and partly attaches to the articular disc?
Which nerve supplies the muscles of mastication?
After a big yawn a patient cannot close the mouth. Where is the head of the mandible?
o: Behind the fossa, against the ear canal
In front of the articular tubercle

q.p: What is the main reinforcing ligament of the TMJ capsule?

t: Joints of the foot: subtalar and transverse tarsal
obj: Identify the subtalar, talocalcaneonavicular and transverse tarsal joints
Describe the ligaments that support the longitudinal arch
Explain inversion and eversion movements
Relate the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament and tibialis posterior to flatfoot

steps.x: It joins the posterior facet of the talus to the calcaneus. Together with the talocalcaneonavicular joint, which lies in front, it allows inversion and eversion of the foot. The lateral, medial and posterior talocalcaneal ligaments reinforce its capsule.
It fills the tarsal sinus between the talus and calcaneus. It is the strongest bond between the two bones. It separates the subtalar joint, behind, from the talocalcaneonavicular joint, in front.

The head of the talus rests on the navicular, the calcaneus and the plantar calcaneonavicular, or spring, ligament. This ligament supports the talar head and the medial longitudinal arch. Its failure contributes to flatfoot.

Formed by the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints, aligned transversely. It works with the subtalar joint in inversion and eversion. The bifurcate ligament, with its calcaneonavicular and calcaneocuboid bands, reinforces it dorsally.

The long plantar ligament runs from the calcaneus to the cuboid and metatarsal bases; the short plantar ligament, from the calcaneus to the cuboid. Both support the lateral longitudinal arch. The plantar aponeurosis acts as a tie between calcaneus and toes.

steps.x: Occipitofrontalis has a frontal and an occipital belly joined by the epicranial aponeurosis. The frontal belly inserts not into bone but into the skin of the eyebrows: it raises them and creates the horizontal forehead wrinkles.

Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids: its palpebral part gently (blinking), its orbital part forcefully. Corrugator supercilii draws the eyebrows medially and downwards (vertical frown lines) and procerus produces the transverse wrinkles over the root of the nose.

Nasalis has a transverse part that compresses the nostril and an alar part that widens it. Depressor septi nasi pulls the septum down. Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi widens the nostril and raises the lip.

Zygomaticus major draws the angle of the mouth upwards and laterally: it is the smiling muscle. Zygomaticus minor and levator labii superioris raise the lip; levator anguli oris raises the corner and risorius pulls it laterally.

Orbicularis oris closes and protrudes the lips. Buccinator presses the cheek against the molars to keep the bolus between the teeth; the parotid duct pierces it. The depressors lower the corner and the lip, mentalis raises and protrudes the lower lip, and platysma tenses the skin of the neck.

All derive from the second pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the facial nerve, which branches within the parotid gland into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches. Peripheral (Bell) palsy affects the whole half of the face, forehead included; a central lesion spares the forehead.

Acting alone, it tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side; both together flex the neck. The accessory nerve (XI) supplies it. Its congenital shortening causes torticollis.

They run from the cervical transverse processes to the ribs: anterior and middle to the 1st, posterior to the 2nd. They raise these ribs in forced inspiration and bend the neck laterally. The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between scalenus anterior and medius, where they can be compressed (thoracic outlet syndrome).

steps.x: It runs from the occipital bone, nuchal ligament and spinous processes C7–T12 to the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula. It arises from spinous processes T7–T12, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest and the lower ribs, and inserts into the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm (climbing, swimming). The thoracodorsal nerve supplies it, and it is used as a flap in reconstructive surgery.

The rhomboids run from spinous processes C7–T5 to the medial border of the scapula: they retract it and hold it against the chest wall. Levator scapulae descends from transverse processes C1–C4 to the superior angle and elevates it. Both rotate the glenoid cavity downwards. The dorsal scapular nerve supplies them.

They run from transverse processes to higher spinous processes: semispinalis (spanning 4–6 vertebrae), multifidus (2–4, best developed in the lumbar region) and rotatores (1–2). They stabilise each segment and rotate the spine. Like all intrinsic muscles, the posterior rami supply them. Lumbar multifidus atrophies in chronic low back pain.

steps.x: The brachial fascia surrounds the arm, and the medial and lateral intermuscular septa, attached to the humerus, divide it into an anterior (flexor) and a posterior (extensor) compartment. Each has its own nerve.

The long head arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and runs in the intertubercular sulcus; the short head, from the coracoid process. It inserts on the radial tuberosity and, through the bicipital aponeurosis, into the forearm fascia. It flexes the elbow and is the most powerful supinator with the elbow flexed. Rupture of the long head gives the "Popeye" sign.

Brachialis runs from the distal half of the anterior humerus to the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna: it is the pure flexor of the elbow, in any forearm position. Coracobrachialis runs from the coracoid to the medial surface of the humerus and flexes and adducts the arm.

The musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7) pierces coracobrachialis, supplies the three flexors and ends as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. The brachial artery descends on the medial side with the median nerve; it is auscultated when measuring blood pressure.

The long head arises from the infraglenoid tubercle and also crosses the shoulder; the lateral and medial heads arise from the humerus, above and below the radial groove. They insert on the olecranon and extend the elbow, helped by anconeus.

The radial nerve supplies triceps and anconeus and winds around the humerus in the radial groove with the deep brachial artery. A humeral shaft fracture can injure it there: wrist drop from paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors, with triceps usually spared.

steps.x: Pectineus, adductor longus, brevis and magnus, gracilis and obturator externus arise from the pubis and ischiopubic ramus and pass to the femur (gracilis to the tibia). They adduct the thigh and stabilise the pelvis during gait. Groin strain in athletes usually involves adductor longus.

steps.t: Adductor magnus and the adductor hiatus
steps.x: It has an adductor part, from the ischiopubic ramus to the linea aspera, and a hamstring part, from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle; its upper portion is called adductor minimus. Between the two insertions lies the adductor hiatus, through which the femoral artery enters the popliteal fossa and becomes the popliteal artery.

The obturator nerve (L2–L4) leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal and divides into an anterior branch, in front of adductor brevis, and a posterior branch, behind it. It supplies the medial compartment except the hamstring part of adductor magnus (tibial); pectineus is usually supplied by the femoral nerve.

Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and the long head of biceps femoris arise from the ischial tuberosity: they extend the hip and flex the knee. The short head arises from the linea aspera and crosses only the knee. Biceps goes to the head of the fibula; semimembranosus, to the medial tibial condyle. The long head of biceps is the one most often injured in sprinting.

The tendons of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert together on the medial surface of the proximal tibia. Each comes from a different compartment and nerve: femoral, obturator and tibial. The anserine bursa beneath them can become inflamed and painful on the medial side of the knee.

The sciatic nerve descends between the hamstrings. Its tibial component supplies semitendinosus, semimembranosus, the long head of biceps and the hamstring part of adductor magnus; the short head of biceps receives the common fibular component. Blood arrives mainly through the perforating branches of the deep femoral artery.

t: Leg: anterior, lateral and posterior compartments
obj: Identify the septa and compartments of the leg and the muscles in each
Describe the action of each group on the ankle and foot
Relate each compartment to its nerve and artery
Explain foot drop, rupture of the calcaneal tendon and compartment syndrome

steps.x: The crural fascia, interosseous membrane and intermuscular septa divide the leg into anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior compartments. They are tight boxes: if the pressure inside one rises (compartment syndrome), it must be decompressed urgently.

Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes. Tibialis anterior also inverts the foot. The extensor retinacula hold their tendons at the ankle.

steps.t: Nerve and artery of the anterior compartment
steps.x: The deep fibular nerve and anterior tibial artery descend on the interosseous membrane. The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, very superficially: its injury (fracture, tight cast, crossing the legs) causes foot drop and a steppage gait.

Fibularis longus and brevis evert the foot, supplied by the superficial fibular nerve. Their tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus under the fibular retinacula. Brevis inserts on the base of the 5th metatarsal, which can be avulsed in an inversion sprain; longus crosses the sole to the 1st metatarsal.
show: Common tendon sheath of fibularis muscles

steps.x: Gastrocnemius and soleus form triceps surae and insert via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon on the calcaneus: they plantarflex the ankle. Gastrocnemius also crosses the knee; soleus is postural and pumps venous blood. If the tendon ruptures, squeezing the calf does not move the foot (Thompson test).

Popliteus unlocks the extended knee. Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus plantarflex and invert; their tendons pass behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum. Tibialis posterior supports the medial arch: its dysfunction causes adult acquired flatfoot.

The tibial nerve supplies both posterior compartments. The popliteal artery divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries; the latter gives the fibular artery, which also supplies the lateral compartment. Behind the medial malleolus, the tibial nerve and posterior tibial artery enter the tarsal tunnel.

obj: Identify the diaphragm, the intercostals and the accessory muscles of respiration
Describe the parts of the diaphragm and the openings that pass through it

steps.x: A musculotendinous dome separating thorax and abdomen. Its sternal, costal and lumbar (crural) parts converge on the central tendon. It is the main inspiratory muscle: when it contracts it descends and increases the vertical diameter of the thorax. The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) supplies it; its irritation causes pain referred to the shoulder.

The inferior vena cava crosses it through the central tendon (T8), the oesophagus through a muscular hiatus in the right crus (T10), and the aorta passes behind it, under the median arcuate ligament (T12). Passage of the stomach through the oesophageal hiatus is a hiatal hernia.

The external intercostals, with fibres running downwards and forwards, raise the ribs in inspiration; the internal intercostals, at right angles, lower them in forced expiration. Between the internal and innermost layers, in the costal groove, run the intercostal vein, artery and nerve: that is why thoracentesis is done just above the upper border of the lower rib.

Transversus thoracis runs from the posterior surface of the sternum to costal cartilages 2–6; the subcostales, near the costal angles, span one or two ribs. Together with the innermost intercostals they form the deepest layer and weakly help to lower the ribs.

The levatores costarum run from transverse processes C7–T11 to the next rib (breves) or the second rib below (longi) and raise it; posterior rami supply them. The serratus posterior muscles are considered accessory, although their real respiratory role is doubtful.

In forced inspiration, the scalenes and sternocleidomastoid raise the sternum and upper ribs, and the pectorals act if the arms are fixed (the patient leans on the hands). Seeing these muscles working at rest is a sign of respiratory distress.
show: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

steps.x: At rest expiration is passive: the elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall is enough. In forced expiration (coughing, blowing, exercise) the abdominal muscles raise intra-abdominal pressure, push the diaphragm upwards and lower the ribs, helped by the internal intercostals.

t: The brain from the inside: nuclei and ventricles

steps.x: The brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata) joins the brain to the spinal cord and contains the cranial nerve nuclei and vital centers. The cerebellum, behind it, coordinates movement; its tonsils can herniate through the foramen magnum when intracranial pressure rises.

The lateral ventricles, one in each hemisphere, communicate through the interventricular foramina with the third ventricle, between the two thalami; this continues through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, in front of the cerebellum. The choroid plexus produces cerebrospinal fluid (about 500 ml a day). Its obstruction causes hydrocephalus.

The caudate nucleus surrounds the lateral ventricle; the putamen and globus pallidus form the lentiform nucleus. Together with the substantia nigra and the subthalamus they control the initiation and scaling of movement: their degeneration produces Parkinson disease (substantia nigra) and Huntington disease (caudate).

In a coronal section the following can be recognized, from medial to lateral: third ventricle, thalamus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus and putamen), external capsule, claustrum and insula. Above, the corpus callosum crosses the midline and forms the roof of the lateral ventricles.
show: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci)

steps.x: The hippocampus, in the wall of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, consolidates memory; the fornix carries its fibers to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus. The amygdala, in front of the hippocampus, processes fear and emotions. Involvement of the hippocampus explains the recent memory loss of Alzheimer disease.

An axial section, such as that of a CT or MRI of the skull, shows in a single plane the frontal horns of the ventricles, the head of the caudate, the lentiform nucleus, the internal capsule shaped like a V open outward, and the thalamus. Try the CT and MRI modes in the Planes tab.

steps.t: The sensory nerves: I, II and VIII
steps.x: The olfactory nerve (I) crosses the cribriform plate of the ethmoid; the optic nerve (II) leaves the orbit through the optic canal toward the chiasm; the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) enters the internal acoustic meatus beside the facial nerve. They are purely sensory nerves.

steps.t: The motors of the eye: III, IV and VI
steps.x: The oculomotor nerve (III) supplies almost all the extraocular muscles, the levator palpebrae and, with parasympathetic fibers, the pupil; the trochlear nerve (IV), the superior oblique; the abducens nerve (VI), the lateral rectus. A lesion of III leaves the eye "down and out" with ptosis and mydriasis.
The largest of the cranial nerves: its three branches (ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular) collect sensation from the face, and the mandibular branch supplies the muscles of mastication.

It leaves the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle, runs through the facial canal of the temporal bone and exits through the stylomastoid foramen to supply the muscles of facial expression. Its peripheral lesion (Bell palsy) paralyzes the whole hemiface.

Glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) exit through the jugular foramen: swallowing, taste from the posterior third of the tongue and the parasympathetic innervation of the thorax and abdomen. The accessory nerve (XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; the hypoglossal nerve (XII), the tongue: if injured, the tongue deviates toward the injured side.

steps.x: The spinal cord lies in the vertebral canal, wrapped in dura, arachnoid and pia mater. In adults it ends at about L1–L2 as the conus medullaris, but the dural sac reaches S2. That is why lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5, with no risk of hitting the cord.

The vertebral column grows more than the cord, so the lumbar and sacral roots run almost vertically down to their intervertebral foramina: they form the cauda equina. Its compression (cauda equina syndrome) causes saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention and is a surgical emergency.

In cross-section the grey matter is H-shaped around the central canal. The posterior horn receives sensory input and the anterior horn holds the motor neurons for skeletal muscle. Between T1 and L2 the intermediolateral nucleus forms the lateral horn, the source of preganglionic sympathetic neurons.

The gracile fasciculus (medial, lower limb) and the cuneate fasciculus (lateral, upper limb, above T6) carry fine touch, vibration and conscious proprioception. They ascend on the same side and cross in the medulla. Their damage causes sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg sign.

The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature; its fibres cross in the anterior white commissure one or two segments above their entry. The spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum, and the lateral corticospinal tract is the main motor pathway. A cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard) causes ipsilateral paralysis and contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

The posterior root is sensory and carries the spinal ganglion, which holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons; the anterior root is motor. They join at the intervertebral foramen to form the spinal nerve, which is mixed. There are 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal.

On leaving, the spinal nerve gives a posterior ramus, for the deep muscles and skin of the back, and an anterior ramus. The anterior rami of T1 to T11 are the intercostal nerves, which run in the costal groove below the vein and artery; the others form the cervical, brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.

obj: Describe how the lumbar plexus forms from the anterior rami of L1–L4 and its relation to psoas major

steps.x: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of L1 to L4, often with a contribution from T12, inside the psoas major muscle. Its branches leave through the lateral border of psoas, its anterior surface or its medial border, and that exit point helps to identify them.

They leave the lateral border of psoas and cross in front of quadratus lumborum. They supply the lower flat abdominal muscles and the suprapubic and inguinal skin; the ilio-inguinal runs through the inguinal canal to the upper thigh and external genitalia. They can be injured in inguinal hernia surgery.

It pierces psoas and descends on its anterior surface. Its genital branch enters the inguinal canal and supplies the cremaster muscle; its femoral branch supplies the skin just below the inguinal ligament. The genital branch is the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex.

It crosses iliacus towards the anterior superior iliac spine and passes under the inguinal ligament next to it. It is purely sensory and supplies the skin of the lateral thigh. Its entrapment, meralgia paraesthetica, causes burning and tingling there; it is typical with tight belts or obesity.

It is the largest branch of the plexus. It runs between psoas and iliacus, passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery and branches in the femoral triangle. It supplies iliacus, pectineus, sartorius and quadriceps; its injury prevents knee extension and abolishes the patellar reflex.
show: Anterior cutaneous branches of femoral nerve

steps.x: It leaves the medial border of psoas, runs along the lateral pelvic wall and passes through the obturator canal. Its anterior and posterior branches straddle adductor brevis and supply the adductors, gracilis and obturator externus. Its injury, sometimes during pelvic surgery, weakens thigh adduction.

steps.x: It arises from the lateral cord (C5–C7), pierces coracobrachialis and descends between biceps and brachialis, which it supplies. It is the nerve of elbow flexion and powerful supination. Above the elbow it becomes superficial as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.

A branch of the posterior cord (C5–C6). It passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. It supplies deltoid, teres minor and the skin over the shoulder. It is injured in surgical neck fractures and shoulder dislocations.

It continues the posterior cord (C5–T1). It runs in the radial groove of the humerus with the profunda brachii artery and supplies triceps and anconeus. A humeral shaft fracture can injure it and cause wrist drop through paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors.

steps.t: Radial nerve at the elbow and forearm
steps.x: In front of the lateral epicondyle it supplies brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus, then divides. The superficial branch is sensory and supplies the lateral dorsum of the hand. The deep branch pierces supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve to the forearm extensors.

steps.x: It is formed by the lateral and medial cords (C6–T1) and gives no branches in the arm. It enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres and supplies almost all the flexors; its anterior interosseous branch supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. It then crosses the carpal tunnel.

A branch of the medial cord (C8–T1). It passes behind the medial epicondyle, where a knock gives the familiar tingling, and supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus. In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, the interossei, the two medial lumbricals and adductor pollicis: its injury causes claw hand.

steps.x: The femoral nerve (L2–L4) supplies quadriceps and sartorius and gives cutaneous branches to the front of the thigh. Its terminal sensory branch, the saphenous nerve, runs through the adductor canal and down the medial leg with the great saphenous vein to the medial border of the foot. It can be injured in varicose vein surgery.

steps.t: Sciatic nerve in the gluteal region
steps.x: It is the thickest nerve in the body (L4–S3). It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below piriformis, and descends deep to gluteus maximus, between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity. Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid it.

In the posterior compartment it supplies the hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris) and the ischial part of adductor magnus. It usually divides at the apex of the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common fibular (peroneal) nerves, although sometimes higher up.

It crosses the popliteal fossa in the midline and descends deep to soleus. It supplies the whole posterior compartment of the leg: gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior and the long flexors (plantarflexion and inversion). It passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum (tarsal tunnel) and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.

It follows the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is subcutaneous, and divides there into superficial and deep fibular nerves. It is the most frequently injured nerve of the lower limb (fibular fractures, casts, leg crossing): it causes foot drop and a steppage gait.

steps.x: The superficial nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis (eversion) and the skin of the dorsum of the foot. It accompanies the small saphenous vein, passes behind the lateral malleolus and supplies the skin of the lateral border of the foot. Being purely sensory, it is used for nerve biopsies and grafts.

t: The motor pathway: from cortex to spinal cord
obj: Locate the primary motor cortex and describe its somatotopic organisation
Trace the corticospinal pathway through the internal capsule, brainstem and spinal cord
Explain the pyramidal decussation and why a brain lesion affects the opposite side of the body
Differentiate the signs of upper and lower motor neuron lesions

steps.x: It occupies the precentral gyrus, in front of the central sulcus (Brodmann area 4). Its map, the motor homunculus, places the face and hand on the lateral surface, with a large area, and the leg and foot in the paracentral lobule on the medial surface. That is why an anterior cerebral artery stroke mainly weakens the opposite leg.

The axons descend through the white matter (corona radiata) and converge in the internal capsule, which the model does not show as a separate piece: it fills the gap between the caudate and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. Corticospinal fibres run in its posterior limb; a small lacunar infarct here causes a pure contralateral hemiparesis.

In the midbrain the corticospinal fibres occupy the middle part of the base of the cerebral peduncle, on each side of the interpeduncular fossa. Behind lies the red nucleus, origin of the rubrospinal tract. A lesion here (Weber syndrome) combines an ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.

In the basilar pons the fibres scatter among the pontine nuclei and regroup in the medullary pyramids. At the medullospinal junction about 85–90 % cross (pyramidal decussation) to form the lateral corticospinal tract; the rest descend uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract. That is why each hemisphere moves the opposite side of the body.

steps.t: Spinal cord: upper and lower motor neuron
steps.x: The corticospinal tracts end, mostly through interneurons, on anterior horn motor neurons, whose axons leave by the anterior root to the muscle. An upper motor neuron lesion causes spasticity, hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign; a lower motor neuron lesion causes flaccid paralysis, atrophy and fasciculations.

Corticonuclear fibres reach the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves, mostly from both hemispheres. The facial nucleus is the key exception: the part that moves the forehead receives fibres from both sides, while the part for the lower face receives only contralateral fibres. That is why a stroke spares the forehead and Bell palsy does not.

The rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal and tectospinal tracts arise in the brainstem and regulate tone, posture and head orientation. The cerebellum and basal nuclei do not project directly to the spinal cord: they adjust movement mainly by acting on the cortex through the thalamus.

q.p: A stroke in the left internal capsule paralyses the lower right face but spares the forehead. Why?

obj: Identify the midbrain, pons and medulla and the cranial nerves that emerge from each
Describe the posterior surface of the brainstem and the floor of the fourth ventricle
Differentiate the vermis, hemispheres and flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum
Relate the signs of cerebellar syndrome to cerebellar function

steps.x: The brainstem has three levels: midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata. It links the cerebrum to the spinal cord and contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III to XII and the respiratory and cardiovascular centres. Behind it, the fourth ventricle separates it from the cerebellum and continues upwards as the cerebral aqueduct.

In front, the cerebral peduncles bound the interpeduncular fossa, where the oculomotor nerve (III) emerges. Behind, the tectum has four colliculi: the superior ones for visual reflexes and the inferior ones in the auditory pathway. The trochlear nerve (IV) is the only cranial nerve that leaves the posterior surface of the brainstem.

Its bulging anterior surface contains fibres that reach the cerebellum through the middle cerebellar peduncles. The trigeminal nerve (V) leaves its lateral surface. At the pontomedullary sulcus emerge the abducens (VI), near the midline, and the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves at the cerebellopontine angle, the site of vestibular schwannoma.

Anteriorly it shows the pyramids, which carry the corticospinal pathway, and beside them the olives. The hypoglossal nerve (XII) emerges between pyramid and olive; the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X) and accessory (XI) nerves emerge behind the olive. The medulla houses the vital centres: compression by tonsillar herniation can stop breathing.

The posterior surface of the pons and upper half of the medulla forms the floor of the fourth ventricle, the rhomboid fossa. Beneath it lie cranial nerve nuclei: abducens, hypoglossal, dorsal vagal and vestibular. The ventricle drains cerebrospinal fluid into the subarachnoid space through its median and lateral apertures.

The cerebellum has a midline vermis and two hemispheres. The primary fissure separates the anterior lobe (central lobule, culmen, anterior quadrangular lobule) from the posterior lobe (declive, semilunar lobules, biventral lobule and tonsil). The vermis controls posture and gait; the hemispheres coordinate fine movements of the limbs on the same side.

The flocculus and nodule form the flocculonodular lobe, connected with the vestibular nuclei: balance and eye movements. The superior cerebellar peduncle is the main output of the cerebellum to the red nucleus and thalamus. A cerebellar lesion causes ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor and nystagmus on the same side.

steps.x: The autonomic system uses a two-neuron chain: a preganglionic neuron in the central nervous system and a postganglionic neuron in a ganglion. The sympathetic arises from the intermediolateral nucleus of T1 to L2 (thoracolumbar); the parasympathetic from brainstem nuclei and S2–S4 (craniosacral). The hypothalamus coordinates both.

On each side of the vertebral bodies runs the sympathetic trunk, a chain of paravertebral ganglia from the skull base to the coccyx. It receives preganglionic fibres through the white rami communicantes (T1–L2) and returns postganglionic fibres to every spinal nerve through the grey rami, for blood vessels, sweat glands and arrector pili muscles.

The cervical ganglia of the trunk supply the head: dilator pupillae, superior tarsal muscle and facial sweat glands. Their interruption, for example by a lung apex tumour (Pancoast), produces ipsilateral Horner syndrome: mild ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis.

Fibres for the abdominal viscera pass through the trunk without synapsing (splanchnic nerves) and end in prevertebral ganglia beside the aorta, such as the coeliac ganglion around the coeliac trunk. The adrenal medulla is the exception: it receives preganglionic fibres directly and releases adrenaline into the blood.

Four cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres. The oculomotor (III), from its accessory nucleus, constricts the pupil and accommodates the lens. The facial (VII), from the superior salivatory nucleus, supplies the lacrimal gland and, through the chorda tympani, the submandibular and sublingual glands. The glossopharyngeal (IX), from the inferior salivatory nucleus, supplies the parotid. The fourth is the vagus.

The vagus (X) is the main parasympathetic nerve. From the dorsal vagal nucleus (cardiac fibres mainly from the nucleus ambiguus) it descends through the neck and thorax to the heart, the bronchi and the gut as far as about the left colic flexure. It slows the heart and stimulates digestion; its sudden activation explains vasovagal syncope.

Neurons of S2–S4 form the pelvic splanchnic nerves. They supply the descending and sigmoid colon, the rectum, the detrusor muscle of the bladder and the erectile tissues: bladder emptying, defecation and erection. Their injury in pelvic surgery can cause urinary retention and erectile dysfunction.

steps.x: The two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx form a ring closed anteriorly at the pubic symphysis. In women the pelvis is wider and lower, the pelvic inlet is oval, the ischial spines are farther apart and the pubic arch exceeds 80°: all of this widens the birth canal.

They join the sacrum to the ischial spine (sacrospinous) and to the ischial tuberosity (sacrotuberous). They convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, through which the pudendal vessels and nerve pass toward the perineum.

The obturator internus lines the lateral wall and its thickened fascia forms the tendinous arch of the levator ani, a band from the pubis to the ischial spine where the pelvic floor is anchored. The piriformis closes the posterior wall.

The levator ani (pubococcygeus, puboanal/puborectalis and iliococcygeus) and the coccygeus form a funnel-shaped hammock that supports the viscera. In the midline it leaves the urogenital hiatus, through which the urethra and vagina pass. The puborectalis sling pulls the rectum forward and forms the anorectal angle, key to continence.

From front to back: bladder, uterus with the vagina, and rectum. The uterus is usually in anteversion (tilted forward over the bladder) and anteflexion. Between the uterus and rectum lies the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity.

The uterus is suspended by the cardinal (Mackenrodt) and uterosacral ligaments, which fix the cervix to the pelvic walls; the round ligament keeps it in anteversion and the broad ligament is a peritoneal fold that carries the vessels. Their weakening, together with that of the levator ani, produces prolapse.

Below the pelvic diaphragm, the superficial perineal space contains the crura of the clitoris with the ischiocavernosus, the vestibular bulbs with the bulbospongiosus, the Bartholin glands and the superficial transverse perineal muscle. All converge on the perineal body, together with the external anal sphincter.

The uterine artery, a branch of the internal iliac, crosses over the ureter ("water under the bridge"), a critical detail in hysterectomy. The pudendal nerve and vessels leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and enter the perineum through the lesser one, wrapping around the ischial spine: this is where the pudendal block is performed in obstetrics.

steps.x: The heart occupies the middle mediastinum, with two thirds to the left of the midline and the apex pointing down, forward and to the left. It receives the venae cavae in the right atrium and the four pulmonary veins in the left; the pulmonary trunk and the ascending aorta leave the ventricles.

They arise from the aortic sinuses, just above the aortic valve. The right coronary runs in the right atrioventricular groove; the left divides into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery, which supplies the anterior part of the septum, and the circumflex. Venous blood returns through the coronary sinus to the right atrium.

A frontal section opens the four cavities. The walls of the left ventricle are about three times thicker than those of the right, because they propel blood into the systemic circulation at higher pressure. The interventricular septum separates the two ventricles.

The tricuspid (right, three leaflets) and mitral (left, two leaflets: anterior and posterior) open in diastole to fill the ventricles and close in systole: their closure produces the first heart sound. The leaflets are held by chordae tendineae to the papillary muscles, which contract to prevent them from prolapsing into the atria.

steps.x: The mouth is bounded by the palate above, the cheeks laterally and the muscular floor below, on which the tongue rests. The hard palate (maxilla and palatine bone) continues posteriorly as the soft palate, which ends in the uvula and rises during swallowing to close off the nasopharynx.

An adult has 32 teeth: in each quadrant two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. They sit in the alveoli, covered by the gingiva. Upper teeth are supplied by branches of the maxillary nerve and lower teeth by the inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve.

They move the tongue as a whole. Genioglossus protrudes it, hyoglossus depresses it, styloglossus retracts and elevates it, and palatoglossus elevates its root. All are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII), except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus.

The superior and inferior longitudinal, transverse and vertical muscles do not attach to bone: they change the shape of the tongue for speech and swallowing. They are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve. If one hypoglossal nerve is injured, the protruded tongue deviates towards the injured side.

In the anterior two-thirds, general sensation travels in the lingual nerve (a branch of V3) and taste in the chorda tympani (VII), which joins the lingual nerve. In the posterior third, the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) carries both. Movement depends on the hypoglossal nerve.

It is the largest salivary gland and lies in front of the ear, over the masseter. Its duct (Stensen's duct) crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar. The facial nerve passes through the gland and divides within it: it must be preserved during parotidectomy.

The submandibular gland wraps around the posterior border of mylohyoid; its duct (Wharton's duct) opens on the sublingual caruncle, beside the frenulum, and is the commonest site of salivary stones. The sublingual gland lies beneath the mucosa of the floor of the mouth. Both receive secretomotor fibres from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani.

steps.x: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavities and receives the auditory tube. The oropharynx, behind the mouth, extends down to the epiglottis. The laryngopharynx descends to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6), where it becomes the oesophagus.

The three constrictors overlap like stacked cups and contract from above downwards to push the bolus. They are supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus. The cricopharyngeal part of the inferior constrictor acts as the upper oesophageal sphincter; just above it, a weak posterior area (Killian's triangle) is where a Zenker's diverticulum forms.

Stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus elevate the pharynx and larynx during swallowing. Stylopharyngeus is the only one supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX); tensor veli palatini by V3; the rest by the vagus. Tensor and levator veli palatini tense and raise the soft palate and open the auditory tube when yawning or swallowing.

The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence ("Adam's apple"). The cricoid, at C6, is the only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway. The arytenoids articulate on it and move the vocal folds. Between thyroid and cricoid, the median cricothyroid ligament is the site of emergency cricothyrotomy.

Posterior crico-arytenoid is the only abductor: it opens the glottis for breathing. Lateral crico-arytenoid and transverse arytenoid close it (adductors). Cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage and tenses the vocal folds (high pitch); vocalis fine-tunes their tension.

All intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus, except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The recurrent nerve ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove behind the thyroid: injury during thyroidectomy causes hoarseness, and bilateral injury can obstruct the airway.

steps.x: It is a muscular tube about 25 cm long that begins at C6, after the pharynx. It descends behind the trachea and through the posterior mediastinum, passes through the diaphragm at the oesophageal hiatus (T10) and ends at the cardia. Its upper third is striated muscle and its lower third smooth muscle.

The oesophagus narrows at its origin, behind the cricoid; where it is crossed by the aortic arch and the left main bronchus; and where it passes through the diaphragm. Swallowed foreign bodies lodge at these points and caustic injuries are worst there.

It has the cardia, the fundus (under the left dome of the diaphragm), the body, the pyloric part (antrum and canal) and the pylorus, whose sphincter controls emptying into the duodenum. The lesser curvature faces right and the greater curvature left. It is supplied by the vagus, which stimulates acid secretion and motility.

The lesser omentum joins the lesser curvature to the liver; the greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature like an apron in front of the intestine. Behind the stomach, the omental bursa separates it from the pancreas: an ulcer of the posterior wall can perforate into it.

The coeliac trunk arises from the aorta at T12 and divides into the left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries. The lesser curvature receives the left and right gastric arteries; the greater curvature, the gastro-omental and short gastric arteries. The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum: a posterior duodenal ulcer can erode it and bleed.

The gastric veins drain into the portal vein. In the lower oesophagus, branches of the left gastric vein (portal system) anastomose with oesophageal veins draining to the azygos (caval system). In portal hypertension these anastomoses dilate into oesophageal varices, which can bleed massively.

Functionally it has eight segments, each with its own portal, arterial and biliary branch; the hepatic veins run between them. Both enter at the hilum together with the bile duct (portal triad). Blood leaves through the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.

The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; it has a fundus, body and neck, which continues as the cystic duct. The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the bile duct, which descends behind the duodenum and the head of the pancreas. In cholecystectomy the cystic artery is identified in the hepatocystic triangle (Calot's triangle).

Retroperitoneal, it crosses the spine at L1–L2. The head sits in the duodenal loop and its uncinate process passes behind the superior mesenteric vessels; the neck lies in front of the origin of the portal vein; the body and tail reach the splenic hilum. It is exocrine (digestive enzymes) and endocrine (insulin and glucagon from the islets).

The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) runs through the gland and joins the bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major papilla in the 2nd part of the duodenum, controlled by the sphincter of Oddi. The accessory duct (of Santorini) opens slightly higher, at the minor papilla. A stone impacted in the ampulla can cause acute pancreatitis.

steps.x: They are retroperitoneal, on either side of the spine between T12 and L3; the right one lies slightly lower because of the liver. They are surrounded by perirenal fat and renal fascia (Gerota's fascia). At the hilum, from front to back, lie the vein, the artery and the renal pelvis.

The renal arteries arise from the aorta at L1–L2; the right one passes behind the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein, which is longer, crosses in front of the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery and receives the left gonadal vein. Its compression between the two arteries (nutcracker syndrome) can cause haematuria and a left varicocele.

The renal artery divides into anterior and posterior branches, which give rise to the segmental arteries. They are end arteries: they do not anastomose with each other, so occlusion of one causes infarction of the segment it supplies. Between the anterior and posterior territories lies a relatively avascular plane useful in renal surgery.

Minor calyces join into major calyces and these into the renal pelvis, which continues as the ureter (≈25 cm). It descends on psoas, crosses the iliac vessels as it enters the pelvis and reaches the bladder. It has three narrowings: the pelvi-ureteric junction, the iliac crossing and the entry into the bladder, where stones lodge in renal colic.

When empty it lies in the pelvis behind the pubis; when full it rises into the abdomen and can be punctured above the pubis without crossing the peritoneum. Inside, the trigone is the smooth area between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. The detrusor muscle contracts during micturition under parasympathetic stimulation (S2–S4).

The female urethra is about 4 cm long, which favours urinary tract infections. The male urethra is about 20 cm long and has three parts: prostatic, membranous (surrounded by the voluntary external sphincter) and spongy, inside the corpus spongiosum of the penis.

steps.x: The testes lie in the scrotum, about 2–3 °C below body temperature, which spermatogenesis requires. The epididymis, on the posterior border, has a head, body and tail: sperm mature and are stored there. The tail continues as the ductus deferens.

The testicular arteries arise from the aorta at L2, a reminder that the testis develops in the lumbar region and descends. The right vein drains into the inferior vena cava and the left, at a right angle, into the left renal vein: this is why varicocele is more common on the left. Cremaster raises the testis (cremasteric reflex).

It ascends in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal, enters the pelvis, crosses above the ureter beside the bladder and widens into an ampulla behind it. Its scrotal segment, easy to palpate, is where vasectomy is performed.

The seminal glands, behind the bladder, provide most of the volume of semen, a fluid rich in fructose. Their duct joins the ampulla of the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate and opens into the prostatic urethra.

It surrounds the prostatic urethra below the bladder neck, in front of the rectum. Its peripheral zone, posteriorly, is palpable on digital rectal examination and is where most carcinomas arise. The transition zone, around the urethra, enlarges in benign hyperplasia and obstructs urine flow.

Two dorsal corpora cavernosa and one ventral corpus spongiosum, which contains the urethra and ends in the glans. During erection, parasympathetic fibres (pelvic splanchnic nerves, S2–S4) dilate the deep arteries and the corpora cavernosa fill; ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus help sustain it. Ejaculation depends mainly on the sympathetic system.

steps.x: It is a pyramid with its apex pointing backwards, formed by seven bones. The medial wall (orbital plate of the ethmoid) is the thinnest. The floor, formed by the maxilla, breaks in blow-out fractures after a direct blow and can trap inferior rectus, limiting upward gaze.

It has three layers: fibrous (sclera and transparent cornea), vascular or uvea (choroid, ciliary body and iris) and neural (retina). The lens, suspended by the zonule, focuses the image; the vitreous body fills the posterior segment. Aqueous humour, made by the ciliary body, drains through the iridocorneal angle: if this is blocked, pressure rises (glaucoma).

The four recti arise from the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit. Medial rectus adducts and lateral rectus abducts. Because the orbit diverges laterally, superior rectus elevates and also adducts, and inferior rectus depresses and adducts. Levator palpebrae superioris opens the eye.

Superior oblique passes through the trochlea and inserts behind the equator: it depresses, abducts and intorts the eye; it acts mainly when looking down and in, as when walking downstairs. Inferior oblique elevates, abducts and extorts.

Rule "LR6 SO4": lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens (VI), superior oblique by the trochlear (IV) and the rest, including levator palpebrae, by the oculomotor (III), which also carries parasympathetic fibres for the pupil and accommodation. A III palsy leaves the eye down and out, with ptosis and a dilated pupil. Corneal sensation travels in the ophthalmic nerve (V1).

The lacrimal gland, in the superolateral orbit, secretes tears, which blinking sweeps medially. They enter the canaliculi through the lacrimal puncta, pass into the lacrimal sac and descend through the nasolacrimal duct to the inferior nasal meatus: this is why the nose runs when crying. Secretion depends on parasympathetic fibres of the facial nerve.

The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the internal carotid. The central retinal artery enters the optic nerve and is an end artery: its occlusion causes sudden painless blindness in one eye. The valveless ophthalmic veins drain into the cavernous sinus, so a facial infection can spread inside the skull.
