steps.x: It is a plate of elastic cartilage covered by skin, except the lobule, which lacks cartilage (fibrofatty tissue). Helix, antihelix, tragus and concha funnel sound into the external acoustic meatus (≈2.5 cm), cartilaginous in its outer third and bony in its inner two-thirds. An undrained haematoma of the auricle leaves a "cauliflower ear".

It separates the external from the middle ear and is tilted. The handle of the malleus, attached to it, forms the umbo, and on otoscopy a cone of light is seen anteroinferiorly. The chorda tympani crosses its inner surface. In otitis media the membrane looks bulging and red.

Malleus, incus and stapes transmit vibration from the eardrum to the oval window, where the base of the stapes fits. Because the eardrum is much larger than the oval window, pressure is amplified about 20 times. In otosclerosis the stapes becomes fixed, causing conductive hearing loss.

steps.x: Tensor tympani (V3) pulls on the malleus and stapedius (VII), the smallest skeletal muscle, damps the stapes in response to loud sounds. A proximal facial palsy causes hyperacusis. The auditory tube equalises pressure with the nasopharynx; in children it is shorter and more horizontal, which favours otitis media.

The bony labyrinth is hollowed out of the petrous part of the temporal bone. The cochlea, with about two and a half turns, contains the organ of Corti and converts sound into impulses. The vestibule (utricle and saccule) detects gravity and linear acceleration; the semicircular ducts detect head rotation.

Cranial nerve VIII runs through the internal acoustic meatus with the facial nerve and reaches the brainstem: the cochlear nerve to the cochlear nuclei and the vestibular nerve to the vestibular nuclei. A vestibular schwannoma, at the cerebellopontine angle, causes progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and unsteadiness.

steps.x: The aorta arises from the left ventricle. The ascending part gives off only the coronary arteries. The arch curves backward and to the left above the left main bronchus and ends at the level of the sternal angle (T4).

From right to left arise the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery. The brachiocephalic trunk divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.

It descends through the posterior mediastinum, to the left of the vertebral bodies. It gives off the posterior intercostal arteries (3rd to 11th), the subcostal arteries, bronchial and oesophageal branches and the superior phrenic arteries. It passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12.

They arise from the anterior surface: the coeliac trunk (T12) supplies the foregut; the superior mesenteric artery (L1), the midgut, as far as the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon; the inferior mesenteric artery (L3), the hindgut.

The inferior phrenic arteries supply the diaphragm. The renal arteries arise at L1–L2; the right one is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava. The gonadal arteries arise at about L2. Four pairs of lumbar arteries supply the posterior abdominal wall.

At L4, at about the level of the umbilicus, the aorta divides into the two common iliac arteries and gives off the small median sacral artery. Abdominal aortic aneurysms are usually infrarenal and may be felt as a pulsatile periumbilical mass.

It continues the axillary artery and descends along the medial side of the arm with the median nerve. The deep brachial artery accompanies the radial nerve in the radial groove. In the cubital fossa it is auscultated, medial to the biceps tendon, when measuring blood pressure.

The deep femoral artery arises about 4 cm below the inguinal ligament and supplies the thigh through the circumflex and perforating arteries. The medial circumflex femoral artery is the main supply of the femoral head: femoral neck fractures can cause avascular necrosis.

The femoral artery runs through the adductor canal and passes through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery. It is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa. Its genicular branches form an anastomotic network around the knee.

The azygos vein ascends to the right of the vertebral bodies, from the ascending lumbar veins, and arches over the right main bronchus at T4 to end in the superior vena cava. The hemi-azygos and accessory hemi-azygos veins, on the left, cross the midline to drain into it.

It collects the posterior intercostal, subcostal, bronchial and oesophageal veins. The right superior intercostal vein drains into the azygos; the left, into the left brachiocephalic vein. Because it links the territories of both venae cavae, it is a key collateral route when one is obstructed.

It forms at L5 from the union of the common iliac veins, to the right of the aorta. It receives the renal veins and, just below the diaphragm, the hepatic veins. It passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm (T8) and enters the right atrium.

The left renal vein is long and crosses in front of the aorta, below the superior mesenteric artery. The right gonadal vein drains directly into the vena cava; the left one into the left renal vein at a right angle. This is why varicocele is much more common on the left.

It passes behind the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve and ascends along the midline of the calf. It pierces the deep fascia and usually ends in the popliteal vein, in the popliteal fossa.

They are paired companion veins of the tibial and fibular arteries and join to form the popliteal vein. Contraction of soleus and gastrocnemius compresses them and pushes blood upward: this is the calf muscle pump. Immobility favours deep vein thrombosis.

The popliteal vein passes through the adductor hiatus and becomes the femoral vein, which receives the deep femoral vein. In the femoral triangle the vein lies medial to the artery. Beneath the inguinal ligament it continues as the external iliac vein.

Perforating veins pierce the deep fascia and connect the superficial and deep systems. Their valves let blood flow only from superficial to deep. If the valves fail, pressure is transmitted to the saphenous veins and varicose veins develop.

Each vertebral artery arises from the subclavian artery, ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 and enters the skull through the foramen magnum. The two join at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.

At the base of the brain, the anterior communicating artery joins the two anterior cerebral arteries and each posterior communicating artery joins the internal carotid to the posterior cerebral artery. This ring can compensate for slow occlusion of one artery, although variants are common.

It is the main continuation of the internal carotid artery. It runs in the lateral sulcus over the insula and supplies most of the lateral surface of the hemisphere: motor and sensory areas for the face and upper limb and, in the dominant hemisphere, the language areas.

steps.x: The thoracic duct (not shown in the model) begins at the cisterna chyli, around L1–L2. It passes through the aortic hiatus, ascends between the aorta and the azygos vein and ends at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins. It drains the whole body except the upper right quadrant.

All lymph from the head and neck reaches the deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein. The jugulodigastric node drains the palatine tonsil. An enlarged left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) may indicate abdominal cancer.

They receive lymph from the upper limb and most of the breast. The pectoral, lateral and subscapular groups drain into the central nodes and these into the apical nodes. In breast cancer the sentinel node is examined to decide on axillary surgery.

The parasternal nodes follow the internal thoracic vessels and receive part of the medial breast. The tracheobronchial and paratracheal nodes drain the lungs towards the bronchomediastinal trunks. The juxta-oesophageal nodes drain the oesophagus.

The pre-aortic nodes (coeliac and mesenteric) collect lymph from the gut and form the intestinal trunk. The lumbar nodes, on both sides of the aorta and vena cava, drain the kidneys, gonads, pelvis and lower limbs. This is why testicular cancer spreads first to lumbar, not inguinal, nodes.

The superficial inguinal nodes receive lymph from the superficial lower limb, the abdominal wall below the umbilicus, the perineum and the lower anal canal. They drain to the deep inguinal nodes and then to the external iliac nodes. The popliteal nodes drain the territory of the small saphenous vein.

The thymus, in the superior mediastinum, matures T lymphocytes and involutes after puberty. The spleen, in the left hypochondrium beneath ribs 9 to 11, filters the blood; its rupture in trauma causes severe bleeding. The tonsils guard the entrance to the pharynx.

It descends in the anterior interventricular sulcus towards the apex. It supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the apex and, through its septal branches, the anterior two thirds of the septum. Proximal occlusion causes an extensive anterior infarct.

t: Goniometry: what it is and how to use it
obj: Identify the parts of the universal goniometer

steps.x: Goniometry measures a joint's range of motion (ROM) in degrees. It helps detect limitations, set goals and track progress. It measures the angle between two bony segments, for example the humerus and forearm at the elbow.

It has a body with a 180° or 360° protractor, a fulcrum or axis, a stationary arm fixed to the body and a moving arm that turns on the fulcrum. The app has a goniometer you place by hand in the Movement tab.

The anatomical position is 0° for almost all movements. You measure from there in each direction: the extended knee is 0° and its flexion is counted from 0°. Fix the patient's position (lying or sitting) and always repeat it.

The fulcrum goes over the joint axis. The stationary arm is aligned with the proximal segment and the moving arm with the distal one, along the midline of each bone. Use palpable bony landmarks, such as the acromion or lateral epicondyle, not the skin outline.

Stabilise the proximal segment with your hand. This prevents compensation, such as pelvic tilt during hip flexion or lumbar extension during shoulder flexion. If the trunk or pelvis moves, the angle you read will be larger than the real one.

Active range is produced by the patient; passive range by the examiner. Passive range is usually slightly larger. At the end of passive range you feel the end feel: soft (tissue approximation), firm (capsule, ligaments, muscle) or hard (bone). An abnormal end feel points to a lesion.

Record side, joint, patient position, active or passive, and the start–end range, for example "right knee, passive flexion, supine: 0–125°". Repeat with the same examiner and position. Differences of about 5° may be measurement error alone.

Supine, arm by the side and forearm supinated. Fulcrum: lateral epicondyle of the humerus. Stationary arm: lateral midline of the humerus, towards the acromion. Moving arm: lateral midline of the radius, towards the radial styloid process. Common error: letting the shoulder flex and move the humerus.

Sitting, forearm resting pronated and fingers relaxed. Fulcrum: ulnar side of the wrist, over the triquetrum. Stationary arm: ulnar midline, towards the olecranon. Moving arm: midline of the 5th metacarpal. Common error: extending the fingers, which tenses the flexors and limits the reading.

Supine, with the knee bent to relax the hamstrings. Fulcrum: greater trochanter. Stationary arm: lateral midline of the pelvis. Moving arm: lateral midline of the femur, towards the lateral epicondyle. Common error: not stabilising the pelvis, which tilts posteriorly and adds lumbar flexion.

Supine, with the hip flexed. Fulcrum: lateral epicondyle of the femur. Stationary arm: lateral midline of the femur, towards the greater trochanter. Moving arm: lateral midline of the fibula, towards the lateral malleolus. Common error: measuring with the hip extended, because a tight rectus femoris limits flexion.

Sitting, with the knee bent at least 30°. Fulcrum: lateral malleolus. Stationary arm: lateral midline of the fibula, towards its head. Moving arm: parallel to the 5th metatarsal. With the knee extended the gastrocnemius limits range; always record the knee position.

steps.x: A dermatome is the area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve, through its posterior root and ganglion. Neighbouring dermatomes overlap, especially on the trunk. That is why a single root lesion usually causes hypoaesthesia, not complete anaesthesia.

The ISNCSCI uses 28 key points per side. C2: at least 1 cm lateral to the occipital protuberance. C3: supraclavicular fossa, at the midclavicular line. C4: over the acromioclavicular joint. C1 has no testable dermatome.

C5: lateral side of the antecubital fossa, just proximal to the crease. C6: dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. C7: dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the middle finger. C8: dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the little finger. T1: medial side of the antecubital fossa, proximal to the medial epicondyle.
show: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand

steps.x: T2: apex of the axilla. T3 to T9 follow the intercostal spaces at the midclavicular line: T4 at nipple level and T6 at the level of the xiphoid process. T10: umbilicus. T11: midway between T10 and T12. T12: midpoint of the inguinal ligament.

L1: halfway between T12 and L2. L2: anteromedial thigh, at mid-height. L3: medial femoral condyle, above the knee. L4: medial malleolus. L5: dorsum of the foot, at the 3rd metatarsophalangeal joint. S1: lateral side of the heel.

S2: midline of the popliteal fossa. S3: ischial tuberosity or infragluteal fold. S4-5: perianal skin, less than 1 cm from the mucocutaneous junction, tested as one point. Preserved sensation here defines an incomplete spinal cord injury.

Each point is tested with light touch (cotton) and pin prick (safety pin), compared with the face. Scale: 0 absent, 1 altered, 2 normal. The sensory level is the most caudal segment with normal sensation. A deficit in a single dermatome suggests radiculopathy, such as L5 in an L4-L5 disc herniation.

q.p: Which dermatome corresponds to the umbilicus?
Where is the key sensory point for C7?
o: Dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
Lateral side of the antecubital fossa
Dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the middle finger
q.en: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

q.p: Which key point lies at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament?
A patient with a disc herniation feels tingling on the lateral side of the heel. Which root is most likely?
Why does a single root lesion rarely cause complete anaesthesia in its dermatome?
o: Because the skin has no pain receptors
Because the spinal ganglion regenerates within hours
Because sensation is carried only by anterior roots

obj: Define a myotome and the 0–5 strength scale
Identify the 10 key muscles of the ISNCSCI classification and their segment
Relate each tendon reflex to its roots
Differentiate an upper from a lower motor neuron lesion

steps.x: A myotome is the group of muscles supplied by one motor root. Strength is graded 0 to 5: 0 no contraction, 1 visible or palpable contraction, 2 full movement with gravity eliminated, 3 against gravity, 4 against some resistance and 5 normal.

C5: elbow flexors (biceps brachii and brachialis). C6: wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis). C7: elbow extensors (triceps brachii). They are tested supine, with the proximal segment stabilised.

C8: flexor digitorum profundus, testing flexion of the distal phalanx of the middle finger. T1: little finger abductors, mainly abductor digiti minimi. Both depend on the inferior trunk of the brachial plexus, through the median and ulnar nerves.
L2: hip flexors (iliopsoas). L3: knee extensors (quadriceps femoris). L4: ankle dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior). In the ISNCSCI all are tested supine.
L5: long toe extensors, mainly extensor hallucis longus. S1: ankle plantar flexors (gastrocnemius and soleus). Weakness of extensor hallucis longus is an early sign of L5 radiculopathy.

Biceps: C5–C6. Brachioradialis: C6. Triceps: C7. Patellar: L3–L4. Achilles: S1. Strike the tendon with the hammer and compare with the other side. A reduced reflex at a single level supports a lesion of that root.

An upper motor neuron lesion (corticospinal tract) gives weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and a Babinski sign. A lower motor neuron lesion (anterior horn, root or nerve) gives flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia or areflexia, atrophy and fasciculations.

q.p: Which key muscle tests the L5 root?
Which key muscle represents C8?
Which roots does the patellar reflex assess?
A patient has no Achilles reflex and struggles to rise on tiptoe. Which root is most likely?
Which finding indicates an upper motor neuron lesion?

t: Palpation of the shoulder and shoulder girdle
obj: Locate the clavicle, the acromioclavicular joint and the acromion along a continuous path
Identify the coracoid process in the deltopectoral groove
Differentiate the greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and bicipital groove using humeral rotation
Relate the spine and angles of the scapula to their approximate vertebral level

steps.x: Patient seated, arms relaxed. Start at the jugular notch of the sternum and slide your fingers laterally along the clavicle. It is subcutaneous along its whole length: convex forward in its medial two thirds and concave in its lateral third.

Follow the clavicle to its lateral end: you will feel a small step or gap, the acromioclavicular joint. Lateral to it lies the acromion, flat and quadrangular. A marked, painful step after a fall onto the shoulder suggests an acromioclavicular dislocation.

From the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the clavicle, move about 2–3 cm down into the deltopectoral groove. Press deeply, in a posterolateral direction: you will feel a bony tip. It is tender to pressure even in healthy people, so palpate gently.

steps.t: Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and bicipital groove
steps.x: Elbow at 90° and arm by the side. Just below the lateral edge of the acromion, palpate the greater tubercle. Rotate the arm slowly in and out: your fingers cross the bicipital groove, holding the tendon of the long head of biceps, and then the more medial lesser tubercle.

Patient seated, viewed from behind. From the acromion, follow the spine of the scapula medially, a subcutaneous bony ridge. It ends at the medial border in a triangular area, the root of the spine, which usually lies at the level of the T3 spinous process.

steps.t: Borders and angles of the scapula
steps.x: Trace the medial border from top to bottom. The superior angle lies near T2 and the inferior angle near T7. If the patient places the hand behind the back, the medial border lifts and is easier to follow. Compare both sides to detect a winged scapula.

q.p: Following the clavicle laterally, which structure marks the small step at its lateral end?
Where is the coracoid process sought?
o: In the supraspinous fossa, from behind
In the deltopectoral groove, about 2–3 cm below the clavicle
In the axilla, over the lateral border of the scapula

q.p: Which tendon lies in the bicipital groove?
Which manoeuvre helps distinguish the greater tubercle, groove and lesser tubercle?
o: Rotating the humerus with the elbow at 90°
Shrugging the shoulder towards the ear

q.p: With the patient upright, at what level does the inferior angle of the scapula usually lie?

t: Palpation of the elbow, wrist and hand
obj: Locate the epicondyles and the olecranon and check their alignment
Identify the radial head using pronation and supination
Differentiate the radial and ulnar styloid processes
Describe the boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox and the bone in its floor
Locate Lister's tubercle, the pisiform and the hook of the hamate

steps.x: Patient seated, elbow flexed to 90° and supported. On each side of the distal humerus palpate the medial epicondyle, more prominent, and the lateral one. Behind lies the olecranon. In flexion they form a triangle; in extension, a straight line. If this is altered, suspect fracture or dislocation.

From the lateral epicondyle, slide your finger about 2 cm distally to a groove and then a rounded surface. Ask the patient to turn the palm up and down: the radial head rotates under your finger. Pain here after a fall on the hand suggests a radial head fracture.

Forearm pronated and supported. Follow the lateral border of the radius to its end: the radial styloid. On the medial side, the ulnar styloid is smaller and more posterior. The radial styloid reaches about 1 cm further distally; this explains why the wrist deviates more to the ulnar side.
show: Radial collateral ligament of wrist joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

steps.x: Ask the patient to extend the thumb. A hollow appears between extensor pollicis longus, behind, and extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus, in front. Distal to the radial styloid, in its floor, lies the scaphoid. Tenderness here after a fall requires ruling out a scaphoid fracture.

On the back of the distal radius, roughly in line with the third metacarpal, palpate a small prominence: the dorsal or Lister's tubercle. The extensor pollicis longus tendon passes around its ulnar side and changes direction there towards the thumb.

Palm up. At the distal wrist crease, at the base of the hypothenar eminence, lies the pisiform, where flexor carpi ulnaris ends. From it, move one fingerbreadth diagonally towards the base of the index finger and press: the hook of the hamate. The ulnar nerve passes between them (Guyon's canal).

q.p: With the elbow flexed to 90°, what shape do the two epicondyles and the olecranon form when viewed from behind?
o: An oblique line towards the radius

q.p: How do you confirm that your finger is on the radial head?
o: By ulnar deviation of the wrist
By asking for pronation and supination of the forearm

q.p: Which bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
Which tendon passes around Lister's tubercle?
Which nerve passes between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate?

t: Palpation of the pelvis and hip
obj: Locate the iliac crest and compare the height of both sides
Identify the ASIS and the PSIS and their use as landmarks
Describe the patient position for palpating the ischial tuberosity
Locate the greater trochanter and the pubic symphysis

steps.x: Patient standing. Place your hands on the waist with the radial border of the index finger resting on top: you are on the iliac crest. Follow it from front to back. Compare the height of both sides with your hands level; a difference may reflect a leg-length discrepancy or scoliosis.

Follow the iliac crest forwards and downwards to its end: the ASIS, very prominent in supine lying. Sartorius and the inguinal ligament arise from it. It is used to measure true lower-limb length, down to the medial malleolus.

Patient standing or prone. Look for the two dimples of the lower back: beneath each lies the PSIS. You can also follow the iliac crest backwards to its end. It usually lies at the level of S2 and is used to assess the sacroiliac joint.

Patient side-lying with hip and knee flexed. In this position gluteus maximus slides upwards and uncovers the tuberosity. Palpate at the middle of the gluteal fold and press upwards. The hamstrings arise here; local pain suggests hamstring tendinopathy or ischial bursitis.

From the iliac crest, move down the lateral thigh about one hand-width. You will find a broad prominence. Rotate the hip in and out: the greater trochanter moves under your fingers. Tenderness here is typical of greater trochanteric pain syndrome.
show: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus muscle

steps.x: Patient supine. Explain what you will do and ask for consent first. From the umbilicus, slide the edge of your hand down the midline until it meets the pubis. On each side lie the pubic tubercles, where the inguinal ligament ends. Compare their heights.

q.p: Which muscle arises from the ASIS?
The dimples of the lower back mark the PSIS. At what level does it usually lie?
Why is the ischial tuberosity palpated with the hip flexed?
o: Because gluteus maximus slides away and uncovers the tuberosity

q.p: Which manoeuvre confirms that you are palpating the greater trochanter?
Between which two points does the inguinal ligament run?

obj: Locate the patella, the patellar tendon and the tibial tuberosity
Find the medial and lateral joint lines with the knee flexed
Identify the fibular head and its relation to the common fibular nerve
Describe the pes anserinus, the iliotibial band and Gerdy's tubercle

steps.x: Patient supine with the knee extended and quadriceps relaxed. Palpate the borders of the patella and its superior and inferior poles. When relaxed, it glides from side to side. Pain when pressing it against the femur points to patellofemoral pain.

From the inferior pole of the patella, follow a firm band downwards: the patellar tendon (ligament). It ends on a prominence on the front of the tibia, the tibial tuberosity. Pain there in active adolescents suggests Osgood-Schlatter disease.

Flex the knee to 90° with the foot on the couch. On each side of the patellar tendon you will feel a soft hollow. Press into it and slide your thumb outwards: the tibial edge is below and the femoral condyle above. Joint-line tenderness is a classic sign of meniscal injury.

On the lateral side, roughly at the level of the tibial tuberosity and slightly posterior, palpate a round prominence: the fibular head. Follow the biceps femoris tendon upwards, which inserts on it. The common fibular nerve winds around the neck just below; avoid pressing it hard.

On the anteromedial tibia, a few centimetres below the medial joint line and medial to the tibial tuberosity, sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert. When the knee flexes against resistance, you will feel their tendons behind. Local pain suggests pes anserine bursitis.

With the knee extended and lifted, the iliotibial band tightens like a strap on the lateral thigh. Follow it to its insertion on Gerdy's tubercle, on the anterolateral tibia, between the tibial tuberosity and the fibular head. Pain over the lateral femoral epicondyle in runners suggests iliotibial band syndrome.

q.p: Where does the patellar tendon end?
Tenderness of the medial joint line with the knee flexed. Which injury does it suggest?
Which nerve winds around the fibular neck, just below its head?
Which muscles form the pes anserinus?
o: Rectus femoris, vastus medialis and sartorius

q.p: Where does the iliotibial band insert?

t: Palpation of the ankle and foot
obj: Differentiate the medial and lateral malleoli by height and position
Locate the sustentaculum tali and the navicular tuberosity from the medial malleolus
Identify the head of the talus using inversion and eversion
Locate the base of the fifth metatarsal and the calcaneal tendon
Apply the palpation points of the Ottawa ankle and foot rules

steps.x: Patient seated with the leg hanging, or supine. Palpate a large prominence on each side of the ankle. The lateral malleolus, of the fibula, is more distal and more posterior than the medial one, of the tibia. Run along the posterior edge and tip of both over their distal 6 cm.

From the tip of the medial malleolus, move down about one fingerbreadth. You will feel a small bony shelf: the sustentaculum tali, part of the calcaneus that supports the talus. The flexor hallucis longus tendon passes beneath it.

From the medial malleolus, move diagonally forwards and downwards about 2–3 cm along the medial border of the foot. The first clear prominence is the navicular tuberosity, where tibialis posterior inserts. Its height above the floor helps assess the medial longitudinal arch.

Place your thumb and index finger just in front of both malleoli. Move the foot into inversion and eversion. In eversion, the head of the talus bulges under the medial thumb; in inversion, under the lateral finger. The position where both sides feel equal is subtalar neutral.

Run along the lateral border of the foot from heel to toes. About halfway you will find an obvious prominence: the base (tuberosity) of the fifth metatarsal, where fibularis brevis inserts. It is a common site of avulsion fracture in inversion sprains.

Patient prone with the feet over the end of the couch. Pinch the calcaneal tendon between thumb and index finger from its insertion on the calcaneus upwards. Feel for gaps or thickening. If squeezing the calf does not produce plantar flexion (Thompson test), suspect a rupture.

q.p: How does the lateral malleolus compare with the medial one?
o: It is more distal and more posterior
It is more proximal and more anterior
It is at the same level
It is more proximal and more posterior

q.p: Which tendon inserts on the navicular tuberosity?
In eversion of the foot, where is the head of the talus felt most?
o: At the base of the fifth metatarsal

q.p: Inversion sprain with pain halfway along the lateral border of the foot. Which structure should you palpate?
Squeezing the calf in prone lying produces no plantar flexion. What does this suggest?

t: Palpation of the spine and level landmarks
obj: Locate the external occipital protuberance and the C7 vertebra
Differentiate C6 from C7 using neck flexion and extension
Relate the scapula, iliac crests and PSIS to their approximate vertebral level
Explain why these level landmarks are approximate and must be confirmed by counting

steps.x: Patient seated with the head slightly flexed. From the nape, move up the midline to the bone: the first clear bump is the external occipital protuberance (inion). The nuchal ligament arises from it and, on each side, the nuchal lines where trapezius and the neck muscles attach.

Move down the midline of the neck. At the base of the neck the C7 spinous process stands out, although T1 is sometimes as prominent or more. To tell them apart, rest one finger on C6 and one on C7 and ask for neck extension: C6 glides forwards and is lost, C7 barely moves.

With the trunk slightly flexed, the spinous processes separate and are easier to count. From C7, move down one by one along the midline. In the mid-thoracic region they are long and oblique: the tip of each lies roughly at the level of the body of the vertebra below.

Patient standing with arms relaxed at the sides. The medial border of the scapula spans roughly T2 to T7. The superior angle lies near T2, the root of the spine near T3 and the inferior angle near T7. If the patient moves the arms, these relations change.

Rest your hands on both iliac crests and bring the thumbs together at the midline: the line joining them (Tuffier's line) crosses roughly L4 or the L4–L5 interspace. Lower down, the line between the two PSIS, under the dimples, lies roughly at the level of S2.

All these landmarks are approximate: they vary with build, posture, age and anatomical variants, and may be off by one level or more. Confirm them by counting spinous processes from C7 or from the sacrum. The intercristal line guides lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or L4–L5, below the end of the spinal cord.

q.p: What happens to C6 and C7 when the neck is extended?
o: C6 glides forwards and is lost; C7 barely moves

q.p: Which level does the line joining the iliac crests roughly cross?
At about what level does the line between both PSIS lie?
With the arms relaxed, which vertebral span does the medial border of the scapula roughly cover?
What is the correct attitude towards these level landmarks?
o: They are exact in all adults
They are approximate and should be confirmed by counting processes
They only work in supine lying
